rationale: A wins because it keeps four clean reporter shapes without dressing guesses up as insight. Its strongest line, "Khan Academy says its AI tutor added weeks of learning — by its own yardstick," names the news and the caveat in the same breath. B has sharper copy in places, but "districts are signing on... based on a study" and the "productive failure and desirable difficulty" detour start importing facts and frames the update did not give it.
gaps_in_A: "30 districts signing on simultaneously" overstates the update; the facts say Khan Academy is rolling out to 30 more districts, not that all signed on simultaneously.
"Khan Academy answers the independent-thinking critics directly" assumes a response posture the facts do not establish; better framed as a question unless the spokesperson is committed.
The adoption-scale angle is viable, but it is the closest to announcement coverage; it needs named districts fast or it becomes "we expanded."
gaps_in_B: "districts are signing on to expand to 1 million students based on a study" invents motivation. The update says the rollout and study are being announced together, not that districts relied on the study.
"a body of research on productive failure and desirable difficulty" may be a real academic frame, but it is not in the supplied update. Good reporter thought, bad blind-grounding discipline.
"Teachers are quietly getting something else" is a cute headline move that implies concealment. The facts only say Khanmigo gives teachers lesson-planning help.
"While VC-backed EdTech companies charge districts" adds outside market contrast without evidence from the update. It may be true, but this set was not licensed to freestyle.
